It was the year תרכ”ה (1865). Four-year-old Reb Shalom Dovber (who grew up to become the Rebbe Rashab) and his older brother, Reb Zalman Aharon, were talking about their Acharon shel Pesach memories.

Reb Shalom Dovber asked his brother, “Do you remember Birchas Kohanim? Do you remember kissing Zeidy, the Tzemach Tzedek’s, tzitzis?”

“Yes!” Reb Zalman Aharon replied, “…it was time for Birchas Kohanim. We were standing near Tatty, and Zeidy motioned for us to come closer to him. We went to Zeidy’s chair and were covered with his tallis. Zeidy followed the pesukim of Birchas Kohanim in the siddur with his finger, and answered the three ‘ameins’ out loud. After davening, Zeidy called me over and allowed me to kiss the tzitzis of his tallis, and then he called you over to kiss them, too!”

As Chabad chassidim, we are very proud of our special

minhagim! There are Chassidishe minhagim for every day of the year, and even more when Yomim Tovim come around! Many of them are specific to a particular Yom Tov,

but some are shayach for every Yom Tov: The unique way that We do Birchas Kohanim, going

on tahalucha, and having special farbrengens. Let’s

One of the most exciting parts of Yom Tov davening is Birchas Kohanim. Our minhag is that all children go under an adult’s tallis during this time, so that we don’t look at the kohanim’s faces while they say these holy brachos.

We also have a special niggun from the Mitteler Rebbe’s Kapelye that the chazzan and kohanim sing before each word. We listen quietly and say “amein” after each of the three brachos.

While the kohanim are singing the niggun before the words “וְיָׂשֵם”, “לְָך“ and “שָׁלֹום”, (but not while they are saying them), we add a special tefillah. This special tefillah is divided into three parts—one for each time the niggun is sung before these words. The Tzemach Tzedek learned about this minhag when he was under the Alter Rebbe’s tallis for Birchas Kohanim, and then he told others about it, too.

These brachos from the kohanim are very powerful and special. Many people even bring their young babies to hear them! Birchas Kohanim takes place during musaf every day of Yom Tov: on Rosh Hashana (Hachayol Issue 621), Yom Kippur (Issue 622) , Sukkos (Issue 623), Shmini Atzeres (Issue 624), Simchas Torah—during shacharis (Issue 624), Pesach (Issue 648) and Shavuos (Issue 656).

Have you ever heard of the mitzvah to walk? That’s right! Walking can sometimes be a mitzvah! For example, it’s a mitzvah to walk to shul for davening, and that’s for all Yidden to do. But we Chabad chassidim have another “walking mitzvah” which happens only three times a year. Can you guess? It’s when we go on tahalucha!

Tahalucha means “a grand march”. Chassidim go on tahalucha on Simchas Torah, Acharon shel Pesach, and the second night of Shavuos. We march to other shuls to bring them extra Yom Tov joy and share with them a vort of the Rebbe’s Torah.

The minhag to go on tahalucha started on Shavuos תשט”ו (1955). That year, Tzeirei Agudas Chabad arranged for some chassidim to go to nearby shuls and say a D’var Torah. At the farbrengen later that day, the Rebbe was very happy. The Rebbe even added that he was jealous of anyone who went! He said l’chaim with them and gave them brachos. From then on, it has become a set minhag.

The Rebbe emphasizes that the steps we take on tahalucha are holy. Therefore, we should take as many of them as possible. The farther we walk, the better! We march with simcha, knowing that each step brings more brachos, more z’chuyos, and more honor.

Some people indeed walk very long distances for tahalucha. For example, if they’re leaving from Crown Heights, they won’t return to 770 until very late at night! This gives the Rebbe tremendous nachas. In fact, in some years, after all of the chassidim had joyously marched back from far-away tahaluchas, the Rebbe himself stood at the steps of 770 to encourage the late-night singing! One year, in א”תנש (1991), the Rebbe did something very unusual. In addition to encouraging the singing, the Rebbe said a short sicha for the tahalucha goers right there on the steps! This happened twice in that same year—once on Acharon shel Pesach, and again on the second night of Shavuos.

Tahalucha isn’t just for fathers or older bochurim. It’s for everyone, from the oldest to the youngest. As children, we chayolim have a special part in the mitzvah of tahalucha. When we visit other Yidden, we can bring extra simcha to them. Make sure to join the tahalucha this Simchas Torah (Hachayol Issue 623), Acharon shel Pesach (Issue 648), and the second night of Shavuos (Issue 656), and bring Chassidishe joy to the Yidden around you!

Further Reading: Toras Menachem vol. 14, p. 119; Toras Menachem vol. 36, pp. 303-304;

There is a special Chabad minhag to hold a farbrengen at the end of each Yom Tov.

At the farbrengen, we sing a niggun from each Rebbe and somebody explains a maamar Chassidus. The farbrengen lasts until Yom Tov is over, followed by maariv right after bentching. We make sure to use the time of the special day for extra singing and Divrei Torah.

When you attend the farbrengen in your city, use your special ko’ach as a chayol to sing with lebedikeit and listen closely to the maamar. Remember, even if you don't understand the maamar, your neshama understands it!

These farbrengens will take place on the second day of Rosh Hashana (Hachayol Issue 621), Simchas Torah (Issue 624), Acharon Shel Pesach (Issue 649), and the second day of Shavuos (Issue 655). Let’s all be there, and give our neshamos this opportunity to enjoy the holy words of Chassidus.
